# Amazing African-Born Actors and Actresses in Hollywood

 #### [1. Djimon Hounsou](link_45) 

    *   Actor
    *   Producer
    *   Director

[Blood Diamond (2006)](link_46)

Djimon Hounsou was born in Cotonou, Benin, in west Africa to Albertine and Pierre Hounsou, a cook. He moved to Lyon, France, when he was 13. Hounsou has graced the catwalks of Paris and London as a popular male model. He has since left his modeling career and has worked on [Gladiator (2000)](link_47) by [Ridley Scott](link_48) and [Amistad (1997)](link_49) by [Steven Spielberg](link_50).

*   
![Image 4: Charlize Theron](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTk5Mzc4ODU0Ml5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTcwNjU1NTI0Mw@@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg) [](link_51)  

 #### [2. Charlize Theron](link_52) 

    *   Producer
    *   Actress
    *   Costume Designer

[Monster (2003)](link_53)

Charlize Theron was born in Benoni, a city in the greater Johannesburg area, in South Africa, the only child of [Gerda Theron](link_54) (née Maritz) and Charles Theron. She was raised on a farm outside the city. Theron is of Afrikaner (Dutch, with some French Huguenot and German) descent, and Afrikaner military figure Danie Theron was her great-great-uncle.  
  
Theron received an education as a ballet dancer and has danced both the "Swan Lake" and "The Nutcracker". There was not much work for a young actress or dancer in South Africa, so she soon traveled to Europe and the United States, where she got a job at the Joffrey Ballet in New York. She was also able to work as a photo model. However, an injured knee put a halt to her dancing career.  
  
In 1994, her mother bought her a one-way ticket to Los Angeles, and Charlize started visiting all of the agents on Hollywood Boulevard, but without any luck. She went to a bank to cash a check for $500 she received from her mother, and became furious when she learned that the bank would not cash it because it was an out-of-state check. She made a scene and an agent gave her his card, in exchange for learning American English, which she did by watching soap operas on television.  
  
Her first role was in the B-film [Children of the Corn III: Urban Harvest (1995)](link_55), a non-speaking part with three seconds of screen time. Her next role was as Helga Svelgen in [2 Days in the Valley (1996)](link_56), which landed her the role of Tina Powers in [That Thing You Do! (1996)](link_57). Since then, she has starred in movies like [The Devil's Advocate (1997)](link_58), [Mighty Joe Young (1998)](link_59), [The Cider House Rules (1999)](link_60), [The Legend of Bagger Vance (2000)](link_61) and [The Italian Job (2003)](link_62). On February 29, 2004, she won her first Academy Award, a Best Actress Oscar for her performance in [Monster (2003)](link_63).

*   
![Image 5: Peter Mensah](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTEyMjE3MTIyNTleQTJeQWpwZ15BbWU3MDc2MDI5ODc@._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg) [](link_64)  

 #### [3. Peter Mensah](link_65) 

    *   Actor

[Jason X (2001)](link_66)

Peter Mensah has been doing martial arts since he was 6 years old, growing up in St. Albans, England, just north of London. A former engineer, Mensah came to Canada 11 years ago. He'd worked for British Gas developing gas fields at Morecambe Bay and had done theatre in school. He comes from an academic family. His father, an architect, relocated with his mother to their native Ghana. He only has two younger sisters. Mensah emigrated from Britain to see the world and it was a toss up whether his destination would be Canada or Australia. The paperwork for Canada came through first.

*   
![Image 6: Omar Sharif at an event for Monsieur Ibrahim (2003)](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTU0ODg3MjM0OF5BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwNTM2MDU0._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg) [](link_67)  

 #### [4. Omar Sharif](link_68) 

    *   Actor
    *   Writer
    *   Producer

[Lawrence of Arabia (1962)](link_69)

[Omar Sharif](link_70), the Egyptian actor best known for playing Sherif Ali in [Lawrence of Arabia (1962)](link_71) and the title role in [Doctor Zhivago (1965)](link_72), was born Michel Demitri Shalhoub on April 10, 1932 in Alexandria, Egypt to Joseph Shalhoub, a lumber merchant, and his wife, Claire (Saada). Of Lebanese and Syrian extraction, the young Michel was raised Catholic. He was educated at Victoria College in Alexandria and took a degree in mathematics and physics from Cairo University with a major. Afterward graduating from university, he entered the family lumber business.  
  
Before making his English-language film debut with "Lawrence of Arabia", for which he earned a Best Supporting Actor Academy Award nomination and international fame, Sharif became a star in Egyptian cinema. His first movie was the Egyptian film [The Blazing Sun (1954)](link_73) ("The Blazing Sun") in 1953, opposite the renowned Egyptian actress [Faten Hamama](link_74) whom he married in 1955. He converted to Islam to marry Hamama and took the name Omar al-Sharif. The couple had one child ([Tarek Sharif](link_75), who was born in 1957 and portrayed the young Zhivago in the eponymous picture) and divorced in 1974. Sharif never remarried.  
  
Beginning in the 1960s, Sharif earned a reputation as one of the world's best known contract bridge players. In the 1970s and 1980s, he co-wrote a syndicated newspaper bridge column for the Chicago Tribune. Sharif also wrote several books on bridge and has licensed his name to a bridge computer game, "Omar Sharif Bridge", which has been marketed since 1992. Sharif told the press in 2006 that he no longer played bridge, explaining, "I decided I didn't want to be a slave to any passion any more except for my work. I had too many passions, bridge, horses, gambling. I want to live a different kind of life, be with my family more because I didn't give them enough time.".  
  
As an actor, Sharif had made a comeback in 2003 playing the title role of an elderly Muslim shopkeeper in the French film [Monsieur Ibrahim (2003)](link_76). For his performance, he won the Best Actor Award at the Venice Film Festival and the Best Actor César, France's equivalent of the Oscar, from the Académie des Arts et Techniques du Cinéma.  
  
Diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2012, Sharif died of a heart attack on July 10, 2015, in Cairo, Egypt.

*   
![Image 9: Jean Reno at an event for Jet Lag (2002)](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/M/MV5BMTgzNjA1MjY2M15BMl5BanBnXkFtZTYwMjgzOTk0._V1_QL75_UX60_CR0,0,60,60_.jpg) [](link_86)  

 #### [7. Jean Reno](link_87) 

    *   Actor
    *   Voice Actor - Dubbing

[Léon: The Professional (1994)](link_88)

Jean Reno was born Juan Moreno y Herrera-Jiménez in Casablanca, Morocco, to Spanish parents (from Andalucía) who moved to North Africa to seek work. His father was a linotypist. Reno settled in France at 17. He began studying drama and has credits in French television and theater as well as films. His first two marriages both ended in divorce, and he had two children with each of them. He keeps homes in Paris and Los Angeles.

Little known by the general public, Moroccan-born Amidou can nevertheless boast an onstage and on screen career spanning almost five decades. **Washington Sixolo** (c.1934 – June 4, 2017), also credited as **Washington Xisolo**, was a South African film and television actor best known to audiences for his role of Jwara on the long-running [SABC 1](link_5)[television series](link_6), _[Emzini Wezinsizwa](link_7)_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-sworld-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-ds-2) He also co-starred as Bhebhe in the 1986 miniseries, _[Shaka Zulu](link_8)_, as well as several international films, including _[Ernest Goes to Africa](link_9)_ (1997) and _[Who Am I?](link_10)_ (1998), opposite [Jackie Chan](link_11).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-sabc-3)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Washington_Sixolo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Sixolo was born in [Springs](link_4) on the [East Rand](link_12), South Africa.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-sabc-3) He began his professional acting career during the late 1970s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-sabc-3) Sixolo was also a founding member of the renowned Kings Messengers Quartet.

## Kings Messengers Quartet

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Washington_Sixolo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Kings Messengers Quartet")]

Together with three [adventist](link_13) friends; Justice Masinga, Alex Maseko and Joseph Mhlanga, he began this exceptional quartet [_[peacock prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Puffery "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] who was great in the sixties and seventies. Beginning at Bethel College, [Butterworth](link_14) in the former [Transkei](link_15) in the early fifties, Washington Sixolo was the main reason why the Kings Messengers earned great recognition in South Africa and abroad. When hearing the Kings Messengers [Quartet](link_16) sing "No Disappointment in Heaven", former [Zambian](link_17) president, [Kenneth Kaunda](link_18), could not resist hearing them in person. He arranged a fully paid trip for this world class quartet [_[peacock prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Puffery "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] to sing for him in his presidential suite and elsewhere in Zambia. Sixolo, still part of the quartet took three new members; Norman Dube (1st [Tenor](link_19)), Mike Thlokoane (2nd Tenor) and Gift Makapela ([Baritone](link_20)) with him to sing for Kaunda in 1970.

Sixolo sang up to the mid seventies for the Kings Messengers before joining the [SABC](link_30) on a fulltime basis. The members of the Kings Messengers Quartet in order of appearances were Alex Maseko (1st tenor), Justice Masinga (2nd tenor), Joseph Mhlanga (baritone), Washington Sixolo (bass), Moses Khumalo (1st tenor), Billy Mahlalela (baritone), Norman Dube (1st tenor), Palmer Paul Kote (2nd tenor), Gift Makapela (baritone), Mike Thlokoane (2nd tenor), Stephen Motha (baritone), Vincent Mvelase (2nd tenor), Zolani Sixolo (1st tenor) and Samson Phakhati ([bass](link_21)). The name Kings Messengers was coined by Moses Khumalo after they were only known as "The quartet" for a while.

Sixolo appeared on 7 of the 8 albums the Kings Messengers made over the years. Only on 1 Kings Messengers album in 1983 did Sixolo not feature. Gift Makapela who toured with Sixolo to Zambia to sing for Kaunda was the leader on this album which was the last Kings Messengers album of all time.

Albums that the Kings Messengers made are: _Soul of Africa_, _Precious Moments with the Kings Messengers Quartet_, _More Songs with the Kings Messengers Quartet_, _The Best of the Kings Messengers Quartet_, _Spiritual Revival_, _Lead Kindly Light_ and _It's Not an Easy Road_.

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Washington_Sixolo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Death")]

Sixolo, who suffered from several illnesses, became seriously ill on June 3, 2017, while at his home in [Orlando West](link_22), [Soweto](link_23).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-sworld-1) He was taken to [Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital](link_24) in Soweto, where he died on June 4, 2017, at the age of 83.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-sworld-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Xisolo#cite_note-ds-2)

**Moira Lister Gachassin-Lafite, Viscountess of [Orthez](link_4)** (6 August 1923–27 October 2007) was a South African-British film, stage and television actress and writer.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moira_Lister&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Lister was born in [Cape Town](link_3) to Major James Lister and Margaret (née Hogan), and educated at the [Parktown Convent of the Holy Family](link_5) in [Johannesburg](link_6).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-:0-1) She studied theatre under Anna Romain Hoffman, who, along with her husband Arthur Hoffman, founded The Johannesburg Repertory Theatre.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moira_Lister&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Lister began her acting career on stage in South Africa and then went on to act in the London theatre at the age of 18.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-fv-2) Lister began working in films in 1943, and appeared in a number of films over several decades. The most notable of these being for [Ealing Studios](link_7), such as _[Another Shore](link_8)_ (1948), _[A Run for Your Money](link_9)_ (1949), _[Pool of London](link_10)_ (1951) and _[The Cruel Sea](link_11)_ (1953). She starred in [Peter Ustinov](link_12)'s long-running 1951 play _[The Love of Four Colonels](link_13)_ in the West End.

She had a regular role in the first series of the [BBC](link_14) radio comedy _[Hancock's Half Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hancock [link_15]'s\_Half\_Hour "Hancock's Half Hour")_ in 1954–55,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-3) and was also one of the girlfriends in _A Life of Bliss_ starring [George Cole](link_16) as David Bliss, a perpetual bachelor. She played Felicity Willow in BBC Radio's comedy _Mr Willow's Wife_.

She starred in the [BBC](link_14) television series _The Whitehall Worrier_ and _The Very Merry Widow_ from 1967 to 1968.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-4) (Later series of this programme were titled _The Very Merry Widow— and How!_) Lister also appeared on various other British TV series such as _[Danger Man](link_17)_ and _[The Avengers](link_18)_ ("The See-Through Man", 1967). In 1980, she made a guest appearance as a film star in the sitcom _[Only When I Laugh](link_19)_.

She was the subject of _[This Is Your Life](link_20)_ in 1971 when she was surprised by [Eamonn Andrews](link_21).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-6)

Lister was still performing until three years before her death, touring with her one-woman show about [Noël Coward](link_22). She belonged to the [British Catholic Stage Guild](link_23).

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moira_Lister&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 1946, Lister went on a date in London with [Neville Heath](link_24), who murdered two women in London only months later.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-:0-1)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-7) Heath was convicted after a sensational trial, and he was hanged in October 1946.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-8)

In 1951, Lister married [Belgo](link_25)-French aristocrat Jacques Gachassin-Lafite, Viscount of [Orthez](link_4), son of André Gachassin-Lafite, Viscount of Orthez and of [Louise van Dievoet](link_26). Jacques was a French [officer](link_27) of the [Spahis](link_28), owner of a champagne vineyard and hero of the [Rif War](link_29); they had two daughters, Chantal and Christobel. Lister also had two granddaughters, Christina d'Orthez and Marina d'Orthez.

Moira Lister died at the age of 84 in 2007. Both she and her husband are interred in the churchyard of St Edward's Catholic Church in [Sutton Green, Surrey](link_30).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-:1-9)

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moira_Lister&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Honours")]

*   [Naledi Theatre Award](link_31), a lifetime achievement award for her services to the theatre in South Africa.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister#cite_note-:1-9)
*   Best Actress of the Year (1971)
*   [Freedom of the City](link_32) of London (2000)

[Omar Sharif](link_52), the Egyptian actor best known for playing Sherif Ali in [Lawrence of Arabia (1962)](link_53) and the title role in [Doctor Zhivago (1965)](link_54), was born Michel Demitri Shalhoub on April 10, 1932 in Alexandria, Egypt to Joseph Shalhoub, a lumber merchant, and his wife, Claire (Saada). Of Lebanese and Syrian extraction, the young Michel was raised Catholic. He was educated at Victoria College in Alexandria and took a degree in mathematics and physics from Cairo University with a major. Afterward graduating from university, he entered the family lumber business.  
  
Before making his English-language film debut with "Lawrence of Arabia", for which he earned a Best Supporting Actor Academy Award nomination and international fame, Sharif became a star in Egyptian cinema. His first movie was the Egyptian film [The Blazing Sun (1954)](link_55) ("The Blazing Sun") in 1953, opposite the renowned Egyptian actress [Faten Hamama](link_56) whom he married in 1955. He converted to Islam to marry Hamama and took the name Omar al-Sharif. The couple had one child ([Tarek Sharif](link_57), who was born in 1957 and portrayed the young Zhivago in the eponymous picture) and divorced in 1974. Sharif never remarried.  
  
Beginning in the 1960s, Sharif earned a reputation as one of the world's best known contract bridge players. In the 1970s and 1980s, he co-wrote a syndicated newspaper bridge column for the Chicago Tribune. Sharif also wrote several books on bridge and has licensed his name to a bridge computer game, "Omar Sharif Bridge", which has been marketed since 1992. Sharif told the press in 2006 that he no longer played bridge, explaining, "I decided I didn't want to be a slave to any passion any more except for my work. I had too many passions, bridge, horses, gambling. I want to live a different kind of life, be with my family more because I didn't give them enough time.".  
  
As an actor, Sharif had made a comeback in 2003 playing the title role of an elderly Muslim shopkeeper in the French film [Monsieur Ibrahim (2003)](link_58). For his performance, he won the Best Actor Award at the Venice Film Festival and the Best Actor César, France's equivalent of the Oscar, from the Académie des Arts et Techniques du Cinéma.  
  
Diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2012, Sharif died of a heart attack on July 10, 2015, in Cairo, Egypt.

Little known by the general public, Moroccan-born Amidou can nevertheless boast an onstage and on screen career spanning almost five decades. Appearing in French films most of the time, he also worked in Morocco, in Tunisia and in American action movies like William Friedkin's 'The Sorcerer' and 'Rules of Engagement', John Frankenheimer's 'Ronin' and Tony Scott's 'Spy Game'. Good-looking and charming, Amidou can easily become frightening and threatening. He is as convincing in the role of a friendly blue collar in 'Smic Smac Smoc' as in that of a dim-witted henchman in 'Fleur d'Oseille'. To be fair, he appeared more often as a dropout or a thug than as positive figure, but this is due to the fact that he started his career in the nineteen sixties, when French cinema was not yet ready to show a North African as just another citizen. Had Amidou debuted later he would have landed more rewarding roles like those now interpreted by Roschdy Zem or Sami Bouajila. Born in 1942 in Rabat, Amidou Ben Messaoud was the son of a justice of the peace and the nephew of the owner of several movie theaters, which gave him the opportunity to see lots of films. On the other hand, the young boy discovered at school that, although he was a bad pupil, he could captivate an audience when, during French lessons, he told and mimicked fables by La Fontaine. Later on, he studied drama at the Conservatoire de Paris and was immediately hired by Jean-Louis Barrault in 1961. Noticed by Jean Genet while he was rehearsing for a bit part, he was given the role of Said instead. At the same time, Claude Lelouch gave him his first part in 'Le Propre de l'Homme' Amidou would then appear in nine other films directed by Lelouch, who also gave him his only starring role in a French movie entitled 'La Vie, l'Amour, la Mort', a pamphlet against the death penalty. Kept busy by the big screen, Amidou was less active in the theatre but played a one man show in the late 1990s ('Le Piston') and held the lead in Mehdi Charef's '1962' in 2005. He also occasionally appeared on TV. Lately Amidou has been honored twice - and quite deservedly so. He was indeed awarded two best actor prizes, one at the Cairo International Festival, for Leila Triquie's 'Poursuite' (2005) and the other at the Tangiers Film Festival for 'Ici et Là' by Rachid Boutounès (2005)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

South African actress (1939–2020)

| Mary Twala-Mhlongo |
| --- |
| Born | Mary Kuksie Twala (1939-09-14)14 September 1939 [Soweto](link_3), [Johannesburg](link_4), [Union of South Africa](link_5) |
| Died | 4 July 2020(2020-07-04) (aged 80)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-1) Parklane Private Hospital, [Johannesburg](link_4), [South Africa](link_6) |
| Other name | Mampinga |
| Occupation | [Actress](link_7) |
| Years active | 1960s – 2020 |
| Notable work | Hlala Kwabafileyo, Molo Fish, Ubizo: The Calling, Yizo-Yizo |
| Spouse | [Ndaba Mhlongo](link_8) (deceased) |
| Family | * [Somizi Mhlongo](link_9) (son) * Archie Mhlongo (son, deceased) * Bahumi Madisakwane (granddaughter) |

**Mary Kuksie Twala**[OIS](link_10) (14 September 1939 – 4 July 2020)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-2) was a South African actress. In 2011, she was nominated for [Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role](link_11).

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Twala&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

Twala featured in several South African local productions. She had a guest role in the first season of _[Generations](link_12)_. In 2007, she starred in local drama, _Ubizo: The Calling_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-3) In 2010, she played a supporting role in _Hopeville_, the film won numerous awards in several festivals and award ceremonies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-4) Twala played "Ma Dolly" in the film, which earned her a Best Supporting Actress nomination in the [6th Africa Movie Academy Awards](link_13).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-5) After undergoing a medical procedure that kept her out of filming for months, Twala made a comeback in _[Vaya](link_14)_ in 2015.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-6)

In 2016, she was one of the ensemble cast in _Comatose_, a film that featured top acts across Africa including [Bimbo Akintola](link_15) and [Hakeem Kae-Kazim](link_16).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-7) In 2017, she played a supporting role in the sport film, _Beyond the River_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-9) By October 2017, it was announced that Twala would feature in a new television drama series on Mzansi Magic, _The Imposter_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-10)

## Selected filmography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Twala&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Selected filmography")]

*   _[Mapantsula](link_17)_ (1988) as Woman in Crowd
*   _[Sarafina!](link_18)_ (1992) as Sarafina's Grandmother
*   _[Beat the Drum](link_19) (2003) as Ntomi_
*   _[Ghost Son](link_20) (2007) as Leleti_
*   _[Life, Above All](link_21) (2010) as Mrs. Gulubane_
*   _[Leading Lady](link_22) (2014) as Sarah Novuka_
*   _Hopeville (2009 TV Series) as Ma Dolly_
*   _[State of Violence](link_23)_ (2010) as Sophie
*   _[This Is Not a Burial, It's a Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Not\_a\_Burial,\_It [link_24]'s\_a\_Resurrection "This Is Not a Burial, It's a Resurrection")_ (2019) as Mantoa
*   _[Black Is King](link_25)_ (2020)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Twala&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Twala was born 14 September 1939 in [Soweto](link_3)[Johannesburg](link_4). She was married to actor [Ndaba Mhlongo](link_8) until his death in 1989. They were the parents of [Somizi Mhlongo](link_9) and Archie Mhlongo (deceased 1985).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-12)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mary_Twala&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Death")]

Twala died on July 4, 2020, at around 11 am at Parklane private hospital, [Johannesburg](link_4).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Twala#cite_note-13) She was laid to rest on July 9, 2020, in [Soweto](link_3). Due to [COVID-19](link_26) regulations, her funeral could be attended by no more than 50 people.

# Trivia

## Amidou

Edit

*   Father of [Souad Amidou](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024850/?ref_=nmtrv_trv).     
*   First Moroccan actor to win a prize at the French Conservatoire National d'Art Dramatique, he was part of the Compagnie Renaud-Barrault's production of Jean Genet's «Les Paravents» in 1968 in Paris.     
*   Worked often for [Claude Lelouch](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0500988/?ref_=nmtrv_trv).     
*   Within the span of five years he worked for Otto Preminger, William Friedkin and John Huston, all iconic directors.

Washington Xisolo was born in Payneville, Springs, South Africa. He was an actor, known for [Who Am I? (1998)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0127357/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Ernest Goes to Africa (1997)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0119068/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Rhodes (1996)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0115335/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He died on 4 June 2017 in Johannesburg, South Africa.

_**The Cruel Sea**_ is a 1953 British [war film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_film "War film") based on the best-selling 1951 [novel of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cruel_Sea_(novel) "The Cruel Sea (novel)") by former naval officer [Nicholas Monsarrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Monsarrat "Nicholas Monsarrat"), though the screenplay by [Eric Ambler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Ambler "Eric Ambler") omits some of the novel's grimmest moments. The film stars [Jack Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Hawkins "Jack Hawkins"), [Donald Sinden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Sinden "Donald Sinden"), [Denholm Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denholm_Elliott "Denholm Elliott"), [Stanley Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Baker "Stanley Baker"), [Liam Redmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_Redmond "Liam Redmond"), [Virginia McKenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_McKenna "Virginia McKenna") and [Moira Lister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister "Moira Lister"). The movie was made by [Ealing Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Studios "Ealing Studios") seven years after the end of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). It was directed by [Charles Frend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Frend "Charles Frend") and produced by [Leslie Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Norman_(director) "Leslie Norman (director)").

The film portrays the conditions in which the [Battle of the Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Atlantic "Battle of the Atlantic") was fought between the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") and Germany's [U-boats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-boat "U-boat"), seen from the viewpoint of the British naval officers and seamen who served in [convoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy "Convoy") escorts.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Cruel_Sea_(1953_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

A voice-over by [Lieutenant-Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_commander_(Royal_Navy) "Lieutenant commander (Royal Navy)") George Ericson, a [British Merchant Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Merchant_Navy "British Merchant Navy") officer in the [Royal Naval Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Naval_Reserve "Royal Naval Reserve"), declares:

> This is a story of the Battle of the Atlantic, the story of an ocean, two ships, and a handful of men. The men are the heroes; the heroines are the ships. The only villain is the sea, the cruel sea, that man has made more cruel...

In late 1939, just as war breaks out, Ericson is recalled to the Royal Navy and given command of HMS _Compass Rose_, a new [Flower-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flower-class_corvette "Flower-class corvette")[corvette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corvette "Corvette") intended for convoy escort duties. His [sub-lieutenants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-lieutenant "Sub-lieutenant"), Lockhart and Ferraby, are both newly commissioned and without experience at sea. The new [first lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_lieutenant#Royal_Navy "First lieutenant"), James Bennett is an abusive [martinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martinet#In_English "Martinet").

Despite these initial disadvantages, the ship's company gains hard experience and becomes an effective fighting unit. At first their worst enemy is the weather, since German submarines lack the range to attack shipping far into the Atlantic. With the [Fall of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_France "Fall of France"), French ports become available to the Germans and U-boats can attack convoys anywhere in the Atlantic – making bad weather the convoys' greatest advantage. Germany is joined in the war by Italy, while the Spanish dictator [Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Franco "Francisco Franco") allows Axis U-boats to use Spanish harbours.

_**Pool of London**_ is a 1951 British [crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_film "Crime film")[film noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_noir "Film noir")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London_(film)#cite_note-5) directed by [Basil Dearden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Dearden "Basil Dearden"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London_(film)#cite_note-6) and starring [Bonar Colleano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonar_Colleano "Bonar Colleano"), [Earl Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Cameron "Earl Cameron") (in his breakthrough role), [Susan Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Shaw "Susan Shaw"), [Renée Asherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9e_Asherson "Renée Asherson") and [Moira Lister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moira_Lister "Moira Lister").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London_(film)#cite_note-BFIsearch-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London_(film)#cite_note-8) It was written by [Jack Whittingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Whittingham "Jack Whittingham") and [John Eldridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Eldridge_(director) "John Eldridge (director)"). Set in post-war [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), the film is of note for portraying the first interracial relationship in [British cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_cinema "British cinema").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London_(film)#cite_note-9)

The film was produced by [Ealing Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing_Studios "Ealing Studios") and released by [General Film Distributors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Film_Distributors "General Film Distributors") on 22 February 1951.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London_(film)#cite_note-Art_&_Hue2-10) It was a commercial and critical success.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pool_of_London_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

The _Dunbar_, a merchant ship, arrives in the [Pool of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_of_London "Pool of London"), bringing a crew of sailors eager to spend their shore leave in the bustling city. Among them are Dan MacDonald, a streetwise American seaman, and Johnny Lambert, his more reserved Jamaican friend. While Dan seeks excitement and quick money, Johnny experiences London from a different perspective, forming a tentative friendship with Pat, a young white woman who shows him kindness despite the racial prejudices of the time.

Dan is approached by a gang of criminals who offer him a large sum of money to smuggle stolen diamonds out of the country. Unaware of the full extent of their crimes, he agrees, seeing it as an easy way to make extra cash. Meanwhile, Johnny spends his time with Pat, enjoying simple moments of companionship but also facing the unspoken social barriers that make their relationship difficult.

The smuggling plot turns violent when one of the gang members kills a watchman, leading to a major police investigation. As the authorities close in, Dan realizes he has been set up and desperately tries to evade capture. He attempts to return to the Dunbar before it leaves port, but the police track him down. In a final act of defiance and redemption, Dan gives himself up to the police, ensuring that Johnny remains uninvolved in the crime.

As the ship prepares to depart, Johnny, deeply affected by Dan’s fate, reflects on his time in London and the challenges he faces as a Black man in British society.

# Biography

## Amidou

## [Overview](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024849/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_ql_1#overview)

*   Born[August 2](https://www.imdb.com/search/name/?birth_monthday=8-2&refine=birth_monthday&ref_=nmbio_bth_md), [1935](https://www.imdb.com/search/name/?birth_year=1935&ref_=nmbio_bth_yr) · [Rabat, French Protectorate in Morocco [now Morocco]](https://www.imdb.com/search/name/?birth_place=Rabat%40%40%40%20French%20Protectorate%20in%20Morocco%20%5Bnow%20Morocco%5D&ref_=nmbio_bth_loc)   
*   Died[September 19](https://www.imdb.com/search/name/?death_date=2013-9-19&refine=death_monthday&ref_=nmbio_dth_md), [2013](https://www.imdb.com/search/name/?death_date=2013&ref_=nmbio_dth_yr) · [Clichy, Hauts-de-Seine, France](https://www.imdb.com/search/name/?death_place=Clichy%40%40%40%20Hauts-de-Seine%40%40%40%20France&ref_=nmbio_dth_loc) (cancer)   
*   Birth name Hamidou Ben Messaoud   

## [Mini bio](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024849/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_ql_1#mini_bio)

*   Little known by the general public, Moroccan-born Amidou can nevertheless boast an onstage and on screen career spanning almost five decades. Appearing in French films most of the time, he also worked in Morocco, in Tunisia and in American action movies like William Friedkin's 'The Sorcerer' and 'Rules of Engagement', John Frankenheimer's 'Ronin' and Tony Scott's 'Spy Game'. Good-looking and charming, Amidou can easily become frightening and threatening. He is as convincing in the role of a friendly blue collar in 'Smic Smac Smoc' as in that of a dim-witted henchman in 'Fleur d'Oseille'. To be fair, he appeared more often as a dropout or a thug than as positive figure, but this is due to the fact that he started his career in the nineteen sixties, when French cinema was not yet ready to show a North African as just another citizen. Had Amidou debuted later he would have landed more rewarding roles like those now interpreted by Roschdy Zem or Sami Bouajila. Born in 1942 in Rabat, Amidou Ben Messaoud was the son of a justice of the peace and the nephew of the owner of several movie theaters, which gave him the opportunity to see lots of films. On the other hand, the young boy discovered at school that, although he was a bad pupil, he could captivate an audience when, during French lessons, he told and mimicked fables by La Fontaine. Later on, he studied drama at the Conservatoire de Paris and was immediately hired by Jean-Louis Barrault in 1961. Noticed by Jean Genet while he was rehearsing for a bit part, he was given the role of Said instead. At the same time, Claude Lelouch gave him his first part in 'Le Propre de l'Homme' Amidou would then appear in nine other films directed by Lelouch, who also gave him his only starring role in a French movie entitled 'La Vie, l'Amour, la Mort', a pamphlet against the death penalty. Kept busy by the big screen, Amidou was less active in the theatre but played a one man show in the late 1990s ('Le Piston') and held the lead in Mehdi Charef's '1962' in 2005. He also occasionally appeared on TV. Lately Amidou has been honored twice - and quite deservedly so. He was indeed awarded two best actor prizes, one at the Cairo International Festival, for Leila Triquie's 'Poursuite' (2005) and the other at the Tangiers Film Festival for 'Ici et Là' by Rachid Boutounès (2005)  
- IMDb mini biography by: Guy Bellinger   

## [Trivia](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024849/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_ql_1#trivia)

*   Father of [Souad Amidou](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024850/?ref_=nmbio_trv).   
*   First Moroccan actor to win a prize at the French Conservatoire National d'Art Dramatique, he was part of the Compagnie Renaud-Barrault's production of Jean Genet's «Les Paravents» in 1968 in Paris.   
*   Worked often for [Claude Lelouch](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0500988/?ref_=nmbio_trv).   
*   Within the span of five years he worked for Otto Preminger, William Friedkin and John Huston, all iconic directors.

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024849/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

Little known by the general public, Moroccan-born Amidou can nevertheless boast an onstage and on screen career spanning almost five decades. Appearing in French films most of the time, he also worked in Morocco, in Tunisia and in American action movies like William Friedkin's 'The Sorcerer' and 'Rules of Engagement', John Frankenheimer's 'Ronin' and Tony Scott's 'Spy Game'. Good-looking and charming, Amidou can easily become frightening and threatening. He is as convincing in the role of a friendly blue collar in 'Smic Smac Smoc' as in that of a dim-witted henchman in 'Fleur d'Oseille'. To be fair, he appeared more often as a dropout or a thug than as positive figure, but this is due to the fact that he started his career in the nineteen sixties, when French cinema was not yet ready to show a North African as just another citizen. Had Amidou debuted later he would have landed more rewarding roles like those now interpreted by Roschdy Zem or Sami Bouajila. Born in 1942 in Rabat, Amidou Ben Messaoud was the son of a justice of the peace and the nephew of the owner of several movie theaters, which gave him the opportunity to see lots of films. On the other hand, the young boy discovered at school that, although he was a bad pupil, he could captivate an audience when, during French lessons, he told and mimicked fables by La Fontaine. Later on, he studied drama at the Conservatoire de Paris and was immediately hired by Jean-Louis Barrault in 1961. Noticed by Jean Genet while he was rehearsing for a bit part, he was given the role of Said instead. At the same time, Claude Lelouch gave him his first part in 'Le Propre de l'Homme' Amidou would then appear in nine other films directed by Lelouch, who also gave him his only starring role in a French movie entitled 'La Vie, l'Amour, la Mort', a pamphlet against the death penalty. Kept busy by the big screen, Amidou was less active in the theatre but played a one man show in the late 1990s ('Le Piston') and held the lead in Mehdi Charef's '1962' in 2005. He also occasionally appeared on TV. Lately Amidou has been honored twice - and quite deservedly so. He was indeed awarded two best actor prizes, one at the Cairo International Festival, for Leila Triquie's 'Poursuite' (2005) and the other at the Tangiers Film Festival for 'Ici et Là' by Rachid Boutounès (2005)

Little known by the general public, Moroccan-born Amidou can nevertheless boast an onstage and on screen career spanning almost five decades. Appearing in French films most of the time, he also worked in Morocco, in Tunisia and in American action movies like William Friedkin's 'The Sorcerer' and 'Rules of Engagement', John Frankenheimer's 'Ronin' and Tony Scott's 'Spy Game'. Good-looking and charming, Amidou can easily become frightening and threatening. He is as convincing in the role of a friendly blue collar in 'Smic Smac Smoc' as in that of a dim-witted henchman in 'Fleur d'Oseille'. To be fair, he appeared more often as a dropout or a thug than as positive figure, but this is due to the fact that he started his career in the nineteen sixties, when French cinema was not yet ready to show a North African as just another citizen. Had Amidou debuted later he would have landed more rewarding roles like those now interpreted by Roschdy Zem or Sami Bouajila. Born in 1942 in Rabat, Amidou Ben Messaoud was the son of a justice of the peace and the nephew of the owner of several movie theaters, which gave him the opportunity to see lots of films. On the other hand, the young boy discovered at school that, although he was a bad pupil, he could captivate an audience when, during French lessons, he told and mimicked fables by La Fontaine. Later on, he studied drama at the Conservatoire de Paris and was immediately hired by Jean-Louis Barrault in 1961. Noticed by Jean Genet while he was rehearsing for a bit part, he was given the role of Said instead. At the same time, Claude Lelouch gave him his first part in 'Le Propre de l'Homme' Amidou would then appear in nine other films directed by Lelouch, who also gave him his only starring role in a French movie entitled 'La Vie, l'Amour, la Mort', a pamphlet against the death penalty. Kept busy by the big screen, Amidou was less active in the theatre but played a one man show in the late 1990s ('Le Piston') and held the lead in Mehdi Charef's '1962' in 2005. He also occasionally appeared on TV. Lately Amidou has been honored twice - and quite deservedly so. He was indeed awarded two best actor prizes, one at the Cairo International Festival, for Leila Triquie's 'Poursuite' (2005) and the other at the Tangiers Film Festival for 'Ici et Là' by Rachid Boutounès (2005)

## [Mini bio](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024849/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_ql_1#mini_bio)

*   Little known by the general public, Moroccan-born Amidou can nevertheless boast an onstage and on screen career spanning almost five decades. Appearing in French films most of the time, he also worked in Morocco, in Tunisia and in American action movies like William Friedkin's 'The Sorcerer' and 'Rules of Engagement', John Frankenheimer's 'Ronin' and Tony Scott's 'Spy Game'. Good-looking and charming, Amidou can easily become frightening and threatening. He is as convincing in the role of a friendly blue collar in 'Smic Smac Smoc' as in that of a dim-witted henchman in 'Fleur d'Oseille'. To be fair, he appeared more often as a dropout or a thug than as positive figure, but this is due to the fact that he started his career in the nineteen sixties, when French cinema was not yet ready to show a North African as just another citizen. Had Amidou debuted later he would have landed more rewarding roles like those now interpreted by Roschdy Zem or Sami Bouajila. Born in 1942 in Rabat, Amidou Ben Messaoud was the son of a justice of the peace and the nephew of the owner of several movie theaters, which gave him the opportunity to see lots of films. On the other hand, the young boy discovered at school that, although he was a bad pupil, he could captivate an audience when, during French lessons, he told and mimicked fables by La Fontaine. Later on, he studied drama at the Conservatoire de Paris and was immediately hired by Jean-Louis Barrault in 1961. Noticed by Jean Genet while he was rehearsing for a bit part, he was given the role of Said instead. At the same time, Claude Lelouch gave him his first part in 'Le Propre de l'Homme' Amidou would then appear in nine other films directed by Lelouch, who also gave him his only starring role in a French movie entitled 'La Vie, l'Amour, la Mort', a pamphlet against the death penalty. Kept busy by the big screen, Amidou was less active in the theatre but played a one man show in the late 1990s ('Le Piston') and held the lead in Mehdi Charef's '1962' in 2005. He also occasionally appeared on TV. Lately Amidou has been honored twice - and quite deservedly so. He was indeed awarded two best actor prizes, one at the Cairo International Festival, for Leila Triquie's 'Poursuite' (2005) and the other at the Tangiers Film Festival for 'Ici et Là' by Rachid Boutounès (2005)

## [Trivia](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024849/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_ql_1#trivia)

*   Father of [Souad Amidou](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024850/?ref_=nmbio_trv).   
*   First Moroccan actor to win a prize at the French Conservatoire National d'Art Dramatique, he was part of the Compagnie Renaud-Barrault's production of Jean Genet's «Les Paravents» in 1968 in Paris.   
*   Worked often for [Claude Lelouch](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0500988/?ref_=nmbio_trv).   
*   Within the span of five years he worked for Otto Preminger, William Friedkin and John Huston, all iconic directors.

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001725/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

[Omar Sharif](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001725/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), the Egyptian actor best known for playing Sherif Ali in [Lawrence of Arabia (1962)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0056172/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and the title role in [Doctor Zhivago (1965)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0059113/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), was born Michel Demitri Shalhoub on April 10, 1932 in Alexandria, Egypt to Joseph Shalhoub, a lumber merchant, and his wife, Claire (Saada). Of Lebanese and Syrian extraction, the young Michel was raised Catholic. He was educated at Victoria College in Alexandria and took a degree in mathematics and physics from Cairo University with a major. Afterward graduating from university, he entered the family lumber business.  
  
Before making his English-language film debut with "Lawrence of Arabia", for which he earned a Best Supporting Actor Academy Award nomination and international fame, Sharif became a star in Egyptian cinema. His first movie was the Egyptian film [The Blazing Sun (1954)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0044429/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) ("The Blazing Sun") in 1953, opposite the renowned Egyptian actress [Faten Hamama](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0357303/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) whom he married in 1955. He converted to Islam to marry Hamama and took the name Omar al-Sharif. The couple had one child ([Tarek Sharif](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0788779/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), who was born in 1957 and portrayed the young Zhivago in the eponymous picture) and divorced in 1974. Sharif never remarried.  
  
Beginning in the 1960s, Sharif earned a reputation as one of the world's best known contract bridge players. In the 1970s and 1980s, he co-wrote a syndicated newspaper bridge column for the Chicago Tribune. Sharif also wrote several books on bridge and has licensed his name to a bridge computer game, "Omar Sharif Bridge", which has been marketed since 1992. Sharif told the press in 2006 that he no longer played bridge, explaining, "I decided I didn't want to be a slave to any passion any more except for my work. I had too many passions, bridge, horses, gambling. I want to live a different kind of life, be with my family more because I didn't give them enough time.".  
  
As an actor, Sharif had made a comeback in 2003 playing the title role of an elderly Muslim shopkeeper in the French film [Monsieur Ibrahim (2003)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0329388/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). For his performance, he won the Best Actor Award at the Venice Film Festival and the Best Actor César, France's equivalent of the Oscar, from the Académie des Arts et Techniques du Cinéma.  
  
Diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2012, Sharif died of a heart attack on July 10, 2015, in Cairo, Egypt.

The **National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Director** is an annual award given by [National Society of Film Critics](link_0) to honor the best film director of the year.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
In this Spanish name, the first or paternal surname is Buñuel and the second or maternal family name is Portolés.
Luis Buñuel


Buñuel in 1929

Born	Luis Buñuel Portolés
22 February 1900
Calanda, Aragon, Spain
Died	29 July 1983 (aged 83)
Mexico City, Mexico
Citizenship	
Spanish (renounced 1949)
Mexican (from 1949)[1]

Education	University of Madrid
Occupation	Filmmaker
Years active	1929–1977
Notable work	Full list
Spouse	Jeanne Rucar ​(m. 1934)​
Children	2, including Juan Luis
Relatives	Diego Buñuel (grandson)

Luis Buñuel Portolés (Spanish: [ˈlwis βuˈɲwel poɾtoˈles]; 22 February 1900 – 29 July 1983) was a Spanish and Mexican filmmaker who worked in France, Mexico, and Spain.[2] He has been widely considered by many film critics, historians, and directors to be one of the greatest and most influential filmmakers of all time.[3] Buñuel's works are known for their avant-garde surrealism which was also infused with political commentary.

Often associated with the surrealist movement, Buñuel's career spanned the 1920s through the 1970s. He collaborated with surrealist painter Salvador Dalí on Un Chien Andalou (1929) and L'Age d'Or (1930).[4] Both are considered masterpieces of surrealist cinema.[5] From 1947 to 1960, he honed his skills as a director in Mexico, making grounded and human melodramas such as Gran Casino (1947), Los Olvidados (1950) and Él (1953).

Buñuel then transitioned to making artful, surrealistic and satirical films. He earned the Palme d'Or at the 1961 Cannes Film Festival for Viridiana (1961), which criticized the Francoist dictatorship. He satirized social conditions in The Exterminating Angel (1962) and The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (1972), the latter of which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. He also directed Diary of a Chambermaid (1964) and Belle de Jour (1967). He earned the National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Director for his final film, That Obscure Object of Desire (1977).[6]

Buñuel earned five Cannes Film Festival prizes, two Berlin International Film Festival prizes, a BAFTA Award and an Academy Award in 1972. Buñuel received numerous honors including National Prize for Arts and Sciences for Fine Arts in 1977, the Moscow International Film Festival Contribution to Cinema Prize in 1979, and the Career Golden Lion in 1982. He was nominated twice for the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1968 and then in 1972. Seven of Buñuel's films are included in Sight & Sound's 2012 critics' poll of the top 250 films of all time.[7][8] Buñuel's obituary in The New York Times called him "an iconoclast, moralist, and revolutionary who was a leader of avant-garde surrealism in his youth and a dominant international movie director half a century later".[9]

Early life and educationedit
Calanda, Spain, in 2013

Buñuel was born on 22 February 1900 in Calanda, a small town in the Aragon region of Spain.[10]: pp.16–17  His father was Leonardo Buñuel, also a native of Calanda, who had left home at age 14 to start a hardware business in Havana, Cuba, ultimately amassing a fortune and returning home to Calanda at the age of 43, in 1898.[11] He married the 18-year-old daughter of the only innkeeper in Calanda, María Portolés Cerezuela.[12] The eldest of seven children, Luis had two brothers, Alfonso and Leonardo, and four sisters: Alicia, Concepción, Margarita and María.[13] He later described his birthplace by saying that in Calanda, "the Middle Ages lasted until World War I".[14]

When Buñuel was four months old, the family moved to Zaragoza, where they were one of the wealthiest families in town.[10]: p.22  In Zaragoza, Buñuel received a strict Jesuit education at the private Colegio del Salvador,[10]: pp.23–36  starting at the age of seven and continuing for the next seven years.[15]: p.22  After being kicked and insulted by the study hall proctor before a final exam, Buñuel refused to return to the school.[16] He told his mother he had been expelled, which was not true; in fact, he had received the highest marks on his world history exam.[14] Buñuel finished the last two years of his high school education at the local public school,[16] graduating at the age of 16. Even as a child, Buñuel was something of a cinematic showman; friends from that period described productions in which Buñuel projected shadows on a screen using a magic lantern and a bedsheet.[17] He also excelled at boxing and playing the violin.[3]

Luis Buñuel (top row, right), Madrid, 1923

In his youth, Buñuel was deeply religious, serving at Mass and taking Communion every day, until, at the age of 16, he grew disgusted with what he perceived as the illogicality of the Church, along with its power and wealth.[18]: p.292 

In 1917, he attended the University of Madrid, first studying agronomy then industrial engineering and finally switching to philosophy.[19] He developed very close relationships with painter Salvador Dalí and poet Federico García Lorca, among other important Spanish creative artists living in the Residencia de Estudiantes, with the three friends forming the nucleus of the Spanish Surrealist avant-garde,[20] and becoming known as members of "La Generación del 27".[21] Buñuel was especially taken with García Lorca, later writing in his autobiography:

We liked each other instantly. Although we seemed to have little in common—I was a redneck from Aragon, and he an elegant Andalusian—we spent most of our time together...We used to sit on the grass in the evenings behind the Residencia (at that time, there were vast open spaces reaching to the horizon), and he would read me his poems. He read slowly and beautifully, and through him I began to discover a wholly new world.[22]: p.62 

Buñuel's relationship with Dalí was somewhat more troubled, being tinged with jealousy over the growing intimacy between Dalí and Lorca and resentment over Dalí's early success as an artist.[18]: p.300 

Buñuel's interest in films was intensified by Fritz Lang's Der müde Tod: "I came out of the Vieux Colombier [theater] completely transformed. Images could and did become for me the true means of expression. I decided to devote myself to the cinema".[23] At the age of 72, Buñuel had not lost his enthusiasm for this film, asking the octogenarian Lang for his autograph.[18]: p.301 

Careeredit
1925–1930: Early French periodedit
Jean Epstein, Buñuel's first film collaborator

In 1925 Buñuel moved to Paris, where he began work as a secretary in an organization called the International Society of Intellectual Cooperation.[24]: p.124  He also became actively involved in cinema and theater, going to the movies as often as three times a day.[25] Through these interests, he met a number of influential people, including the pianist Ricardo Viñes, who was instrumental in securing Buñuel's selection as artistic director of the Dutch premiere of Manuel de Falla's puppet-opera El retablo de maese Pedro in 1926.[26]: p.29 

He decided to enter the film industry and enrolled in a private film school run by Jean Epstein and some associates.[25] At that time, Epstein was one of the most celebrated commercial directors working in France, his films being hailed as "the triumph of impressionism in motion, but also the triumph of the modern spirit".[27] Before long, Buñuel was working for Epstein as an assistant director on Mauprat (1926) and La chute de la maison Usher (1928),[28] and also for Mario Nalpas on La Sirène des Tropiques (Siren of the Tropics) (1927), starring Josephine Baker.[29] He appeared on screen in a small part as a smuggler in Jacques Feyder's Carmen (1926).[30]

When Buñuel derisively rejected Epstein's demand that he assist Epstein's mentor, Abel Gance, who was at the time working on the film Napoléon, Epstein dismissed him angrily, saying "How can a little asshole like you dare to talk that way about a great director like Gance?"[26]: p.30  then added "You seem rather surrealist. Beware of surrealists, they are crazy people."[31]

After parting with Epstein, Buñuel worked as film critic for La Gaceta Literaria (1927) and Les Cahiers d'Art (1928).[26]: p.30  In the periodicals L'Amic de les Arts [ca] and La gaseta de les Arts [ca], he and Dalí carried on a series of "call and response" essays on cinema and theater, debating such technical issues as segmentation, découpage, the insert shot and rhythmic editing.[32] He also collaborated with the celebrated writer Ramón Gómez de la Serna on the script for what he hoped would be his first film, "a story in six scenes" called Los caprichos.[26]: pp.30–31  Through his involvement with Gaceta Literaria, he helped establish Madrid's first cine-club and served as its inaugural chairman.[33]

Un Chien Andalou (1929)edit
Salvador Dalí

After his apprenticeship with Epstein, Buñuel shot and directed a 16-minute short, Un Chien Andalou, with Salvador Dalí. The film, financed by Buñuel's mother,[34] consists of a series of startling images of a Freudian nature,[35] starting with a woman's eyeball being sliced open with a razor blade. Un Chien Andalou was enthusiastically received by the burgeoning French surrealist movement[36] and continues to be shown regularly in film societies.[37] The script was written in six days at Dalí's home in Cadaqués. In a letter to a friend written in February 1929, Buñuel described the writing process:

We had to look for the plot line. Dalí said to me, 'I dreamed last night of ants swarming around in my hands', and I said, 'Good Lord, and I dreamed that I had sliced somebody or other's eye. There's the film, let's go and make it.'[38]

Un Chien Andalou (1929)

In deliberate contrast to the approach taken by Jean Epstein and his peers, which was to never leave anything in their work to chance, with every aesthetic decision having a rational explanation and fitting clearly into the whole,[39] Buñuel and Dalí made a cardinal point of eliminating all logical associations.[40] In Buñuel's words: "Our only rule was very simple: no idea or image that might lend itself to a rational explanation of any kind would be accepted. We had to open all doors to the irrational and keep only those images that surprised us, without trying to explain why".[22]: p.104 

It was Buñuel's intention to outrage the self-proclaimed artistic vanguard of his youth, later saying: "Historically the film represents a violent reaction against what in those days was called 'avant-garde,' which was aimed exclusively at artistic sensibility and the audience's reason."[41] Against his hopes and expectations, the film was a popular success with the very audience he had wanted to insult.[4]Roger Ebert called it one of the most famous short films of the century.[42] Buñuel exclaim in exasperation: "What can I do about the people who adore all that is new, even when it goes against their deepest convictions, or about the insincere, corrupt press, and the inane herd that saw beauty or poetry in something which was basically no more than a desperate impassioned call for murder?"[43]

Although Un Chien Andalou is a silent film, during the original screening (attended by the elite of the Parisian art world), Buñuel played a sequence of phonograph records which he switched manually while keeping his pockets full of stones with which to pelt anticipated hecklers.[44] After the premiere, Buñuel and Dalí were granted formal admittance to the tight-knit community of Surrealists, led by poet André Breton.[45]

L'Age d'Or (1930)edit
Marie-Laure de Noailles was a prominent patron of avant-garde artists, who received L'Age d'Or as a birthday gift from her husband, Charles.[46]

Late in 1929, on the strength of Un Chien Andalou, Buñuel and Dalí were commissioned to make another short film by Marie-Laurie and Charles de Noailles, owners of a private cinema on the Place des États-Unis and financial supporters of productions by Jacques Manuel, Man Ray and Pierre Chenal.[24]: p.124  At first, the intent was that the new film be around the same length as Un Chien, only this time with sound. But by mid-1930, the film had grown segmentally to an hour's duration.[24]: p.116  Anxious that it was over twice as long as planned and at double the budget, Buñuel offered to trim the film and cease production, but Noailles gave him the go-ahead to continue the project.[24]: p.116 

The film, L'Age d'Or, was begun as a second collaboration with Dalí, but, while working on the scenario, the two had a falling out; Buñuel, who at the time had strong leftist sympathies,[47] desired a deliberate undermining of all bourgeois institutions, while Dalí, who eventually supported the Spanish fascist Francisco Franco and various figures of the European aristocracy, wanted merely to cause a scandal through the use of various scatological and anti-Catholic images.[48] The friction between them was exacerbated when, at a dinner party in Cadaqués, Buñuel tried to throttle Dalí's girlfriend, Gala, the wife of Surrealist poet Paul Éluard.[49] In consequence, Dalí had nothing to do with the actual shooting of the film.[50]: pp.276–277  During the course of production, Buñuel worked around his technical ignorance by filming mostly in sequence and using nearly every foot of film that he shot. Buñuel invited friends and acquaintances to appear, for nothing, in the film; for example, anyone who owned a tuxedo or a party frock got a part in the salon scene.[24]: p.116 

A film called L'Age d'or, whose non-existent artistic quality is an insult to any kind of technical standard, combines, as a public spectacle, the most obscene, disgusting and tasteless incidents. Country, family, and religion are dragged through the mud.[51]

— Excerpt from Richard Pierre Bodin's review in Le Figaro, 7 December 1930.

L'Age d'Or was publicly proclaimed by Dalí as a deliberate attack on Catholicism, and this precipitated a much larger scandal than Un Chien Andalou.[52] One early screening was taken over by members of the fascist League of Patriots and the Anti-Jewish Youth Group, who hurled purple ink at the screen[53] and then vandalised the adjacent art gallery, destroying a number of valuable surrealist paintings.[54] The film was banned by the Parisian police "in the name of public order".[55] The de Noailles, both Catholics, were threatened with excommunication by The Vatican because of the film's blasphemous final scene (which visually links Jesus Christ with the writings of the Marquis de Sade), so they made the decision in 1934 to withdraw all prints from circulation, and L'Age d'Or was not seen again until 1981, after their deaths,[56] although a print was smuggled to England for private viewing.[57] The furor was so great that the premiere of another film financed by the de Noailles, Jean Cocteau's The Blood of a Poet, had to be delayed for over two years until outrage over L'Age d'Or had died down.[58] To make matters worse, Charles de Noailles was forced to withdraw his membership from the Jockey Club.[59]

Concurrent with the succès de scandale, both Buñuel and the film's leading lady, Lya Lys, received offers of interest from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and traveled to Hollywood at the studio's expense.[60] While in the United States, Buñuel associated with other celebrity expatriates including Sergei Eisenstein, Josef von Sternberg, Jacques Feyder, Charles Chaplin and Bertolt Brecht.[30] All that was required of Buñuel by his loose-ended contract with MGM was that he "learn some good American technical skills",[61] but, after being ushered off the first set he visited because the star, Greta Garbo, did not welcome intruders, he decided to stay at home most of the time and only show up to collect his paycheck.[62] His only enduring contribution to MGM came when he served as an extra in La Fruta Amarga, a Spanish-language remake of Min and Bill.[63] When, after a few months at the studio, he was asked to watch rushes of Lili Damita to gauge her Spanish accent, he refused and sent a message to studio boss Irving Thalberg stating that he was there as a Frenchman, not a Spaniard, and he "didn't have time to waste listening to one of the whores".[64]: p.18  He was back in Spain shortly thereafter.[60]

1931–1937: Spainedit

Spain in the early 1930s was a time of political and social turbulence.[65] Due to both a surge in anti-clerical sentiment and a longrunning desire for retribution for the corruption and malfeasance of the extreme right and their supporters in the church, Anarchists and Radical Socialists sacked monarchist headquarters in Madrid and proceeded to burn down or otherwise wreck more than a dozen churches in the capital. Similar revolutionary acts occurred in many other cities in southern and eastern Spain, in most cases with the acquiescence and occasionally with the assistance of the official Republican authorities.[66]

Buñuel's future wife, Jeanne Rucar, recalled that during that period, "he got very excited about politics and the ideas that were everywhere in pre-Civil War Spain".[67] In the first flush of his enthusiasm, Buñuel joined the Communist Party of Spain (PCE) in 1931,[47]: pp.85–114  though later in life he denied becoming a Communist.[68]: p.72 

Group of Hurdanos early in the 20th century

In 1932, Buñuel was invited to serve as film documentarian for the celebrated Mission Dakar-Djibouti, the first large-scale French anthropological field expedition, which, led by Marcel Griaule, unearthed some 3,500 African artifacts for the new Musée de l'Homme.[69] Although he declined, the project piqued his interest in ethnography. After reading the academic study, Las Jurdes: étude de géographie humaine (1927) by Maurice Legendre [es; fr; pt], he decided to make a film focused on peasant life in Las Hurdes, perhaps the poorest comarca in Extremadura, one of Spain's poorest regions.[70] The film, called Las Hurdes: Tierra Sin Pan (1933), was financed on a budget of 20,000 pesetas donated by a working-class anarchist friend named Ramón Acín, who had won the money in a lottery.[71] In the film, Buñuel matches scenes of deplorable social conditions with narration that resembles travelogue commentary delivered by a detached-sounding announcer,[72] while the soundtrack thunders inappropriate music by Brahms.[73]

French director François Truffaut began to assiduously go to the movies at age seven. He was also a great reader but not a good pupil. He left school at 14 and started working. In 1947, aged 15, he founded a film club and met [André Bazin](link_52), a French critic, who became his protector. Bazin helped the delinquent Truffaut and also when he was put in jail because he deserted the army. In 1953 Truffaut published his first movie critiques in "Les Cahiers du Cinema." In this magazine Truffaut, and some of his friends as passionate as he was, became defenders of what they call the "author policy". In 1954, as a test, Truffaut directed his first short film. Two years afterwords he assisted [Roberto Rossellini](link_53) with some later abandoned projects.  
  
The year 1957 was an important one for him: he married [Madeleine Morgenstern](link_54), the daughter of an important film distributor, and founded his own production company, Les Films du Carrosse; named after [Jean Renoir](link_55)'s [The Golden Coach (1952)](link_56). He also directed [Les mistons (1957)](link_57), considered the real first step of his cinematographic work. His other big year was 1959: the huge success of his first full-length film, [The 400 Blows (1959)](link_58), was the beginning of the New Wave, a new way of making movies in France. This was also the year his first daughter, [Laura Truffaut](link_59), was born.  
  
From 1959 until his death, François Truffaut's life and films are mixed up. Let's only note he had two other daughters [Eva Truffaut](link_60) (b. 1961) and Josephine (b. 1982, with French actress [Fanny Ardant](link_61)). Truffaut was the most popular and successful French film director ever. His main themes were passion, women, childhood and faithfulness.

The master filmmaker Roberto Rossellini, as one of the creators of neo-realism, is one of the most influential directors of all time. His neo-realist films influenced France's nouvelle vague movement in the 1950s and '60s that changed the face of international cinema. He also influenced American directors, including [Martin Scorsese](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000217/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk).  
  
He was born into the world of film, making his debut in Rome on May 8, 1906, the son of Elettra (Bellan), a housewife, and Angiolo Giuseppe "Beppino" Rossellini, the man who opened Italy's first cinema. He was immersed in cinema from the beginning, growing up watching movies in his father's movie-house from the time that film was first quickening as an art form. Italy was one of the places were movie-making matured, and Italian film had a huge influence on [D.W. Griffith](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000428/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and other international directors. Between the two world wars, Hollywood would soon dictate what constituted a "well-made" film, but Rossellini would be one of the Italian directors who once again put Italy at the forefront of international cinema after the Second World War.  
  
His training in cinema was thorough and extensive and he became expert in many facets of film-making. (His brother [Renzo Rossellini](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0744021/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), also was involved in the industry, scoring films.) He did his apprenticeship as an assistant to Italian filmmakers, then got the chance to make his first film, a documentary, "Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune", in 1937. Due to his close ties to [Benito Mussolini](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0615907/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk)'s second son, the critic and film producer [Vittorio Mussolini](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0615910/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), he flourished in fascist Italy's cinema. Once Il Duce was deposed, Rossellini produced his first classic film, the anti-fascist [Rome, Open City (1945)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0038890/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) ("Rome, Open City") in 1945, which won the Grand Prize at Cannes. Two other neo-realist classics soon followed, [Paisan (1946)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0038823/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) ("Paisan") and [Germany Year Zero (1948)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0039417/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) ("Germany in the Year Zero"). "Rome, Open City" screenwriters [Sergio Amidei](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0024847/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Federico Fellini](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000019/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) were nominated for a Best Writing, Screenplay Oscar in 1947, while Rossellini himself, along with Amidei, Fellini and two others were nominated for a screen-writing Oscar in 1950 for "Paisan".  
  
"I do not want to make beautiful films, I want to make useful films," he said. Rossellini claimed, "I try to capture reality, nothing else." This led him to often cast non-professional actors, then tailor his scripts to their idiosyncrasies and life-stories to heighten the sense of realism.  
  
With other practitioners of neo-realism, [Vittorio De Sica](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001120/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Luchino Visconti](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0899581/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), film was changed forever. American director [Elia Kazan](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0001415/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) credits neo-realism with his own evolution as a filmmaker, away from Hollywood's idea of the well-made film to the gritty realism of [On the Waterfront (1954)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0047296/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk).  
  
Rossellini had a celebrated, adulterous affair with [Ingrid Bergman](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0000006/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) that was an international scandal. They became lovers on the set of [Stromboli (1950)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0041931/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) while both were married to other people and Bergman became pregnant. After they shed their spouses and married, producing three children, history repeated itself when Rossellini cheated on her with the Indian screenwriter [Sonali Senroy DasGupta](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0784452/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) while he was in India at the request of Prime Minister [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0624587/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) to help revitalize that country's film industry. It touched off another international scandal, and Nehru ousted him from the country. Rossellini later divorced Bergman to marry Das Gupta, legitimizing their child that had been born out-of-wedlock.  
  
Rossellini continued to make films until nearly his death. His last film [The Messiah (1975)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0077925/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) ("The Messiah"), a story of The Passion of Christ, was released in 1975.  
  
Roberto Rossellini died of a heart attack in Rome on June 3, 1977. He was 71 years old.
